description: PVCs, accelerated ventricular rhythm, VT, torsades, and VFib

questions.stem: Premature ventricular contractions (PVCs) are characterized by:

options.text: Wide QRS (>80-100ms in children) with no preceding P wave and compensatory pause
Narrow QRS with abnormal P wave morphology
Delta wave and short PR interval
Sawtooth pattern in the baseline

questions.explanation: PVCs arise below the bundle of His, causing abnormal ventricular depolarization that appears as a wide, bizarre QRS complex. There's no preceding P wave because the impulse originates in the ventricle. The compensatory pause is usually 'full' (interval containing PVC equals 2x baseline R-R) because the PVC doesn't reset the SA node.
questions.clinical_pearl: PVC QRS width: Adult >120ms, Child >80-100ms (depending on age). The wide QRS reflects slow cell-to-cell conduction rather than rapid His-Purkinje conduction.

questions.stem: A healthy 8-year-old has occasional PVCs (<1% burden) on Holter monitor. Echo is normal. The child is asymptomatic. What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start beta-blocker therapy
Reassurance - isolated PVCs in structurally normal hearts are usually benign
Refer for catheter ablation
Restrict all physical activity

questions.explanation: Isolated, unifocal PVCs in children with structurally normal hearts and low burden (<5-10%) are typically benign. No treatment or activity restriction is needed. Follow-up echo may be reasonable to ensure ongoing normal LV function if PVCs persist.
questions.clinical_pearl: Benign PVC features: Unifocal, disappear with exercise, no symptoms, normal heart, low burden (<10%). Concerning features: Multifocal, increase with exercise, symptoms, structural disease, high burden (>20%).

questions.stem: Which feature distinguishes a PVC from an aberrantly conducted PAC?

options.text: PVC is always followed by a T wave of opposite polarity
PVC always has a narrower QRS
Aberrant PAC always has a compensatory pause
PVC has no preceding P wave and typically has LBBB morphology or bizarre appearance

questions.explanation: Key differences: 1) PVC has no preceding P wave; aberrant PAC has a premature P wave (may be in T wave), 2) Aberrant PAC typically shows RBBB morphology (right bundle has longer refractory period); PVC morphology varies by origin but often shows LBBB pattern if from RV, 3) PVC has full compensatory pause; PAC has incomplete pause.
questions.clinical_pearl: Search for the hidden P wave! If you find a premature P distorting the preceding T wave followed by a wide QRS, it's aberrancy, not a PVC.

questions.stem: PVCs occurring every other beat is termed:

options.text: Couplets
Ventricular trigeminy
Ventricular bigeminy
Non-sustained VT

questions.explanation: PVC patterns: Bigeminy = every other beat is a PVC, Trigeminy = every third beat is a PVC, Couplets = two PVCs in a row, Triplets = three PVCs in a row. Three or more consecutive PVCs at rate >100 bpm is ventricular tachycardia.
questions.clinical_pearl: Pattern terminology: Bi- = every 2nd beat, Tri- = every 3rd beat, Quadri- = every 4th beat. Couplet = 2 in a row, NSVT = 3+ in a row (<30 sec), Sustained VT = >30 sec or requiring intervention.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old athlete with palpitations has 25% PVC burden on Holter. Echo shows borderline low EF of 50%. What is the most concerning finding and recommended action?

options.text: The EF is normal; reassurance only
This is a normal finding in athletes; no action needed
High PVC burden may be causing LV dysfunction; consider treatment with beta-blockers or ablation
Immediate ICD implantation is indicated

questions.explanation: High PVC burden (>10-20%) can cause PVC-induced cardiomyopathy, which is reversible with successful treatment. The borderline EF suggests early cardiomyopathy. Treatment options include beta-blockers or catheter ablation. With successful PVC suppression, LV function typically normalizes.
questions.clinical_pearl: PVC-induced cardiomyopathy threshold: Generally >10-20% burden, though some patients are more susceptible. The good news: it's reversible! Suppress the PVCs, save the heart.

questions.stem: What does it mean when PVCs are described as 'unifocal'?

options.text: All PVCs have identical morphology, suggesting single site of origin
PVCs occur in only one lead
Only one PVC is seen on the entire recording
PVCs are suppressed with exercise

questions.explanation: Unifocal PVCs all look the same because they originate from the same ventricular location. Multifocal PVCs have different morphologies, indicating multiple sites of origin - this is generally more concerning and may indicate more diffuse myocardial disease.
questions.clinical_pearl: Unifocal = benign feature. Multifocal = concerning feature. When evaluating PVCs, always report: unifocal vs multifocal, frequency/burden, patterns (couplets, runs), and response to exercise.

questions.stem: An asymptomatic 10-year-old has exercise testing. At rest, frequent PVCs are seen. During exercise, PVCs completely disappear. What does this suggest?

options.text: High-risk PVCs requiring immediate treatment
Benign PVCs - suppression with exercise is reassuring
Catecholaminergic polymorphic VT
Underlying structural heart disease

questions.explanation: PVCs that suppress with exercise (when sinus rate exceeds PVC focus rate) are generally benign. PVCs that increase or become more complex with exercise are more concerning and may indicate catecholaminergic VT or arrhythmogenic cardiomyopathy. Exercise testing is useful for risk stratification.
questions.clinical_pearl: Exercise testing for PVCs: Suppression with exercise = reassuring. New or worsening PVCs with exercise = concerning for CPVT or structural disease. Always include exercise testing in the workup!

questions.stem: A 15-year-old with known hypertrophic cardiomyopathy has wide complex tachycardia at 180 bpm. Blood pressure is 70/50 mmHg and the patient is confused. What is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: Amiodarone 150mg IV over 10 minutes
Adenosine 6mg IV push
Synchronized cardioversion
Vagal maneuvers

questions.explanation: This patient has unstable VT (hypotension, altered mental status) in the setting of structural heart disease. Immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated. Adenosine is not first-line for wide complex tachycardia and vagal maneuvers won't work for VT. Amiodarone takes too long for an unstable patient.
questions.clinical_pearl: Unstable wide complex tachycardia = synchronized cardioversion NOW. Signs of instability: Hypotension, Altered mental status, Chest pain, Acute heart failure. Don't delay for diagnosis or drugs!

questions.stem: What differentiates monomorphic VT from polymorphic VT?

options.text: Monomorphic is always faster than polymorphic
Monomorphic has uniform QRS morphology; polymorphic has beat-to-beat QRS variation
Polymorphic is always associated with structural heart disease
Monomorphic requires cardioversion; polymorphic requires defibrillation

questions.explanation: Monomorphic VT has consistent QRS morphology throughout (stable reentrant circuit). Polymorphic VT shows continuously changing QRS complexes (shifting activation, often more unstable). Polymorphic VT with prolonged QT is called Torsades de Pointes. Polymorphic VT is generally more dangerous.
questions.clinical_pearl: Polymorphic VT significance: Check the baseline QT! If QTc is prolonged → Torsades (treat with magnesium, avoid QT-prolonging drugs). If QTc is normal → usually ischemia or CPVT.

questions.stem: Torsades de pointes is characterized by:

options.text: Regular sawtooth pattern
Monomorphic wide complex tachycardia at 150 bpm
Irregular narrow complex tachycardia
Polymorphic VT with twisting QRS axis around the baseline and prolonged baseline QTc

questions.explanation: Torsades de pointes ('twisting of the points') is polymorphic VT characterized by: 1) QRS complexes that appear to twist around the isoelectric baseline, 2) Occurs in the setting of prolonged QT interval (acquired or congenital LQTS), 3) Often initiated by a PVC with long-short sequence.
questions.clinical_pearl: Torsades = polymorphic VT + long QT. The treatment is different from typical VT! Magnesium is first-line, plus address the underlying QT prolongation.

questions.stem: A patient with drug-induced QT prolongation develops Torsades de pointes and is hemodynamically stable with brief, self-terminating episodes. What is the most appropriate treatment?

options.text: IV magnesium sulfate, stop offending drug, correct electrolytes, consider overdrive pacing
Amiodarone IV loading dose
Procainamide IV infusion
Verapamil IV

questions.explanation: Torsades treatment differs from typical VT! 1) IV Magnesium 25-50 mg/kg (even with normal Mg levels), 2) Stop QT-prolonging drugs, 3) Correct K+ to high-normal (4.5-5 mEq/L), 4) If persistent, overdrive pacing (shortens QT). Avoid Class I/III antiarrhythmics (amiodarone, procainamide) - they prolong QT!
questions.clinical_pearl: Torsades treatment: Magnesium, Magnesium, Magnesium! Also: stop offending drug, correct K+ to high-normal, overdrive pace if needed. DON'T give typical antiarrhythmics - they make it worse!

options.text: Complete absence of electrical activity (flat line)
Regular wide complex tachycardia at 200 bpm
Narrow complex tachycardia with visible P waves
Chaotic, irregular waveforms with no identifiable QRS complexes

questions.explanation: VF shows completely chaotic, irregular electrical activity with no organized QRS complexes. The amplitude may be coarse (higher amplitude, better prognosis for successful defibrillation) or fine (lower amplitude, worse prognosis). VF produces no cardiac output - it's a form of cardiac arrest.
questions.clinical_pearl: VF vs asystole: VF = chaotic activity (defibrillate!). Asystole = flat line (CPR + epinephrine, check lead placement). VF has better prognosis if defibrillated quickly.

questions.stem: What is the underlying electrophysiologic mechanism of ventricular fibrillation?

options.text: Multiple wandering reentrant wavelets causing chaotic, disorganized ventricular activation
Single stable reentrant circuit
Enhanced automaticity of a single focus
Complete AV nodal block

questions.explanation: VF represents the ultimate breakdown of organized electrical activity. Multiple reentrant wavelets wander through the ventricle in a chaotic pattern, constantly splitting and colliding. No organized contraction can occur, resulting in no cardiac output. Defibrillation works by simultaneously depolarizing all cells, allowing organized activity to resume.
questions.clinical_pearl: Defibrillation = 'electrical reset.' By depolarizing everything at once, it gives the SA node a chance to resume control. The key is delivering enough energy to capture all the chaotic wavelets.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old has sudden cardiac arrest during basketball, resuscitated from VF. Echo shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis and long-term management?

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy; heart transplant evaluation
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; ICD implantation for secondary prevention
Commotio cordis; no further intervention needed
Long QT syndrome; beta-blocker therapy only

questions.explanation: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is the leading cause of sudden cardiac death in young athletes in the US. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy is classic. Survivors of SCA require ICD for secondary prevention (very high recurrence risk). Family screening is also essential.
questions.clinical_pearl: Causes of SCA in young athletes (US): HCM most common, then ARVC, anomalous coronaries, channelopathies, commotio cordis. All survivors need thorough workup and usually ICD.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old is struck in the chest by a baseball and immediately collapses. CPR is started and AED reveals VF. The patient is successfully defibrillated. Echo and ECG are normal. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Brugada syndrome
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Commotio cordis - VF triggered by mechanical impact during vulnerable period
Blunt cardiac injury with contusion

questions.explanation: Commotio cordis is VF triggered by blunt chest impact during the vulnerable period of repolarization (T wave). It typically occurs with projectiles (baseball, hockey puck, lacrosse ball) in young males. Cardiac evaluation is normal. Most survive if defibrillated within 3 minutes. Prevention: chest protectors in at-risk sports.
questions.clinical_pearl: Commotio cordis window: Impact must occur during the ascending T wave (~20-30ms vulnerable period). It's about timing, not impact force. Chest protectors don't completely prevent it.
